title: Input Validation & Sanitization
summary: The discipline of validating untrusted input at every trust boundary, and why allowlisting beats blocklisting as a default technique.

slides.markdown:
Nearly every major vulnerability class — injection, buffer overflows, path traversal, XSS — starts the same way: **data from outside the system's control was trusted without being checked.** Input validation is the discipline of closing that gap, and it is the single most foundational secure-coding practice, underneath almost every other topic in this group.

The two ideas that matter most: validate at **every** trust boundary a piece of data crosses, not just the outermost one, and prefer **allowlisting** (defining what's acceptable) over **blocklisting** (defining what's forbidden) as the default technique, because a blocklist can only ever cover the attacks someone already thought of.

slides.subTitle: Not just the UI
slides.markdown:
A **trust boundary** is any point where data crosses from a context you don't control into one you do — a user's browser to your API, one internal service to another, a message queue to a consumer, even a config file to the code that parses it. Each crossing is a place where the data could be malformed, malicious, or simply not what the receiving code assumes.

The common mistake is validating only once, at the outermost boundary — say, the public API gateway — and treating everything downstream as safe because "it already passed validation." But a request that legitimately passed the gateway's checks can still carry a value that's dangerous to a specific downstream service in a way the gateway had no reason to check for, and an internal service reachable by *other* internal services (not just through the gateway) never gets that check applied to those other callers at all.

The rule that scales: **every component validates the input it receives, regardless of what validation happened upstream.** It's redundant in the common case and exactly the layer that saves you in the uncommon one.

| | Allowlist (positive validation) | Blocklist (negative validation) |
|---|---|---|
| Defines | What's explicitly permitted; reject everything else | What's explicitly forbidden; permit everything else |
| Coverage | Complete by construction — anything not on the list is rejected | Only as complete as the list of known-bad patterns someone thought to add |
| Fails safe? | Yes — an unanticipated input is rejected by default | No — an unanticipated attack technique is permitted by default |
| Example | A username field: allow only `a-z, 0-9, underscore`, reject anything else | A search filter: block the literal string `<script>`, permit everything else |

The blocklist example above is trivially bypassed — `<ScRiPt>`, a different tag entirely, or an encoded variant all slip through a blocklist looking for one exact string, while an allowlist restricting to a known-safe character set has no such gap, because it never has to anticipate the attack, only define what legitimate input looks like. Allowlisting is the default recommendation precisely because it fails safe against inputs nobody thought of yet.

slides.sectionTitle: Type, length, format, and range checks
slides.markdown:
Concrete validation usually stacks a few narrow checks rather than one broad rule:

- **Type** — is this actually an integer, not a string that happens to contain digits? Type coercion bugs (a string silently interpreted as a number, or vice versa) are a real source of logic errors and, in some languages, security issues.
- **Length** — bound both minimum and maximum. An unbounded string field is a resource-exhaustion vector on its own, independent of any other attack.
- **Format** — does a value that claims to be an email, a date, or a phone number actually match that shape? A regex or parser-based check, not just "contains an @ sign."
- **Range** — is a number within a sane bound for its meaning? An age field accepting `-5` or `9999` is a validation gap even though both are syntactically valid integers.

Each check alone is narrow, but they compose: a field can pass a type check and still be a length bomb, or pass a length check and still be out of range. Real validation applies all four dimensions that are relevant to the field, not just the first one you happen to think of.

slides.subTitle: Three different jobs, often confused
slides.markdown:
These three terms get used interchangeably in casual conversation, but they solve different problems and mixing them up is a real source of bugs:

- **Validation** — deciding whether input is acceptable at all. The outcome is binary: accept or reject. It never modifies the data.
- **Sanitization** — modifying input to remove or neutralize dangerous parts while keeping the rest, rather than rejecting it outright. Stripping HTML tags from a comment field is sanitization.
- **Encoding** — transforming data for the specific context it's about to be placed into, so that context can't misinterpret it as something other than data — HTML-encoding a value before inserting it into a page so `<` becomes `<` and can't be parsed as a tag.

The common bug pattern: sanitizing input on the way *in* and assuming that's sufficient protection on the way *out*, when the actual defense against XSS is contextual **encoding at output time**, not sanitization at input time — a value that was safely sanitized for one context can still be dangerous when later rendered into a different one (HTML vs. a JavaScript string vs. a URL).

slides.sectionTitle: Client-side validation is UX, not security
slides.markdown:
Client-side validation (a browser form refusing to submit an empty field, JavaScript flagging an invalid email format before the request is sent) is genuinely valuable — it gives immediate feedback and reduces round trips for honest mistakes. It is not, and cannot be, a security control.

The reason is structural, not a matter of writing better client-side code: **an attacker doesn't use your form.** They send a request directly to your API — via `curl`, a script, or a modified browser request — bypassing whatever JavaScript validation exists entirely, because that JavaScript never runs at all in that path. Any validation that lives only on the client is invisible and irrelevant to that request.

The rule this implies is unconditional: **every security-relevant validation must be enforced server-side**, regardless of what the client also checks. Client-side validation can duplicate the server-side rule for a better user experience, but the server-side check is the one that actually matters, and skipping it because "the form already validates this" is a direct path to a vulnerability.

slides.sectionTitle: Allowlist validation for a username field
Validation at trust boundaries between internal services
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A subtlety that separates a strong answer from a textbook one: trust boundaries aren't only "external user to system" — they exist **between internal services too**, and it's tempting to skip validation there because "it's an internal call, we control both ends."

That reasoning breaks in exactly the scenario that matters most: if one internal service is compromised (through any means — a dependency vulnerability, a leaked credential, a different unvalidated input elsewhere), every other service that blindly trusts calls from it inherits that compromise immediately, with no additional validation standing in the way. This is the input-validation analogue of the zero-trust principle covered in network security: internal network position (or, here, "it's another service we wrote") is not a substitute for validating what actually arrives.

In practice this means internal APIs validate their inputs with the same rigor as public-facing ones, even when the caller is "trusted" — because the actual security property you want is bounded blast radius if any single component is compromised, not an assumption that no component ever will be.

A field can pass every syntactic check — right type, right length, right format — and still be semantically wrong for what the business logic needs, which is a gap pure format validation doesn't close. An email field can contain a syntactically perfect email address that belongs to someone else entirely; a "quantity" field can be a valid positive integer that's still absurd for the context (ordering 50,000 units of a product with 12 in stock).

This is why validation is layered in mature systems: **structural validation** (type, format, range) happens close to the input boundary and rejects malformed data early and cheaply, while **business-rule validation** (does this quantity make sense given current inventory, does this transfer amount respect this account's limits) happens deeper in the application logic, often requiring a lookup or a stateful check that structural validation alone can't perform.

Treating structural validation as sufficient on its own is a common gap: an attacker doesn't need to break the format of a field to abuse it, they just need a value that's syntactically valid and semantically harmful.

slides.sectionTitle: Validating once at the gateway and trusting it everywhere downstream
slides.markdown:
The pitfall: an API gateway validates incoming requests, and every service behind it is written assuming that validation has already happened, so none of them check their own inputs. This works right up until it doesn't — a new internal caller is added that bypasses the gateway, a bug in the gateway's validation logic lets something through, or a message arrives via a queue or event bus that never passed through the gateway's code path at all.

When any of those happen, every downstream service that skipped its own validation is now exposed with no defense at all — the gateway wasn't wrong to validate, but treating that single check as the *only* check turned one component's mistake or blind spot into a system-wide vulnerability.

The fix is the trust-boundary discipline from earlier in this topic, applied without exception: every service validates what it receives, including from other internal services and other trusted-seeming sources, because the gateway's validation is a good first filter, not a substitute for defense in depth.
